text: I hired 12 engineers last year. Here are 5 lessons nobody tells you about hiring 👇 First, attitude beats skills almost every single time, because skills can be taught but attitude rarely can. text: We migrated our billing database to a new cluster last quarter and I want to share what we measured. p99 latency went from 180ms to 95ms, mostly by removing an N+1 query in the invoice renderer and adding one composite index. The table holds 1.2 billion rows, so we backfilled in batches of 50 thousand with a throttle tied to replica lag. Two things surprised us: vacuum was the real bottleneck, not the copy itself, and our connection pool was sized for the old cluster. The runbook and the dashboards are linked in the comments below.

We missed our pipeline target three quarters in a row, and the cause was not effort. Our attribution model double counted webinar leads, so we kept funding the channel that looked best on paper. Fixing the model cut reported pipeline by a third overnight, and it was the most useful week of the year.

Deleting them and rewriting two runbooks cut night pages by more than half and nobody missed a real outage. text: I hired 12 engineers last year. Here are the three places our interview loop was wrong, with data. Our take-home assignment predicted nothing: scores had no correlation with first-year reviews across the cohort. The system design round favoured people who had seen the question before. And reference calls only helped when we asked about a specific project instead of general strengths. We replaced the take-home with a paid pairing session and the signal improved.

label: highlight
text: We moved our search index from one large node to three smaller ones and measured the effect for a month. Query latency at the 99th percentile improved, but indexing throughput dropped because every write now fans out to replicas. The fix was batching writes on the client and accepting a few seconds of staleness for non-critical fields. Costs went down a little, operational complexity went up a lot. I would do it again, but only with the batching in place from day one.
